items.prompt: Define government economic policy.
items.canonical_answer: Actions and decisions intended to influence economic activity towards chosen objectives.
marking_guidance: Definition: economic actions/decisions 1; qualifier: intended objectives 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Identify whether price stability is a policy objective or instrument.
items.canonical_answer: An objective (1).
marking_guidance: Characteristic: intended outcome, 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain why a tax change intended to support employment is an instrument rather than the employment objective itself.
items.canonical_answer: The tax change is the means used to influence decisions (1), while employment is the outcome sought (1).
marking_guidance: Context: tax/employment; reasoning: means 1; result: outcome distinction 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain one possible benefit of employment policy where productive labour is unused.
items.canonical_answer: Useful work can raise output and household earnings (1), because available labour is applied to needed production rather than remaining idle (1).
marking_guidance: Benefit for household/economy 1; because: productive use of available labour 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain one limitation of increasing demand to support employment when production capacity is already constrained.
items.canonical_answer: Extra spending may put pressure on prices rather than produce much extra output (1), because firms cannot expand supply sufficiently, limiting the policy’s employment benefit (1).
marking_guidance: Limitation for economy 1; because: capacity constraint 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Evaluate whether an economy should use additional spending solely to maximise near-term output when capacity is constrained and hardship is unevenly distributed.
items.canonical_answer: Argument for: extra spending can raise output where some workers and resources remain unused, and can target sectors with spare capacity. Argument against: capacity constraints can create price pressure, while benefits may miss people in hardship or create external costs. Judgement: target feasible productive and access needs while checking capacity, distribution and external costs. The condition for broad benefit is a real response whose gains reach intended groups, rather than output ambition alone.
marking_guidance: Argument for: demand/output mechanism up to 3; argument against: capacity/distribution costs up to 3; judgement with capacity and shared-benefit condition up to 2 = 8.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum
items.repair_note: Step-6 Claude review: added standard examined content (named points, definitions, lists) missing from notes; corrected definition cards and template-garbled answers; removed author/tooling wording and invented/original labels.

items.prompt: Explain why population rising while real output is unchanged does not itself show economic growth.
items.canonical_answer: Economic growth concerns real output rather than the number of people (1); with unchanged output and more people, output per person falls (1).
marking_guidance: Confusion: population versus real production; boundary/test: output measure, 1 each.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Define fiscal policy and monetary policy, showing how their instruments differ.
items.canonical_answer: Fiscal instruments use public spending and taxes; monetary instruments use monetary and credit conditions such as interest rates.
marking_guidance: Meaning: policy instrument families 1; distinguishing feature: spending/tax versus money/credit 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain why raising public spending and changing the central-bank policy rate are different policy families.
items.canonical_answer: Public spending is fiscal (1), whereas the rate is a monetary instrument, even though both can affect economic demand (1).
marking_guidance: Difference/distinguishing test: actual instrument, 1 each.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain why a government income-tax reduction is fiscal even if it aims to increase household borrowing and spending.
items.canonical_answer: The instrument is taxation (1), so it is fiscal; the intended spending effect does not turn it into an interest-rate or money instrument (1).
marking_guidance: Context: tax change; reasoning: instrument base 1; result: fiscal despite outcome 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum
items.repair_note: Step-6 Claude review: added standard examined content (named points, definitions, lists) missing from notes; corrected definition cards and template-garbled answers; removed author/tooling wording and invented/original labels.

items.prompt: Explain the error in calling a central-bank interest-rate decision fiscal because it affects firms.
items.canonical_answer: The instrument concerns monetary and credit conditions (1), so it is monetary; fiscal uses spending and taxes, not the general fact of affecting business (1).
marking_guidance: Confusion: outcome versus instrument; boundary/test: rate versus spending/tax, 1 each.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Identify the tax classification whose proportion of income paid rises as income rises.
items.canonical_answer: Progressive tax (1).
marking_guidance: Characteristic: progressive share pattern, 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain why direct/indirect and progressive/proportional/regressive are different tax classification axes.
items.canonical_answer: Direct/indirect concern the tax base and collection route (1), whereas the other terms concern how the income share changes (1).
marking_guidance: Difference/distinguishing test: route/base versus share pattern, 1 each.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain why a 10 percent charge producing N$400 on N$4,000 and N$1,000 on N$10,000 is proportional.
items.canonical_answer: Both payments are 10 percent of the base (1), so different cash amounts do not change the equal-rate pattern (1).
marking_guidance: Context: incomes; reasoning: common ratio 1; result: proportional, not equal amount 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain why proportional tax does not require each taxpayer to pay the same cash amount.
items.canonical_answer: It requires the same rate relative to the base (1), so a larger income at that rate produces a larger payment (1).
marking_guidance: Confusion: rate versus amount; boundary/test: tax/base ratio, 1 each.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Define a government budget.
items.canonical_answer: A plan of public revenue and expenditure for a stated period.
marking_guidance: Meaning: revenue/spending plan 1; qualifier: public finances and period 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain how lower household income tax may influence business demand.
items.canonical_answer: Initial change: more disposable income remains (1); households may spend some on firms’ output, supporting demand if they choose to do so (1).
marking_guidance: Initial change 1; mechanism/effect: conditional disposable-income spending route 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain the fiscal meaning of planned revenue N$120 million and expenditure N$132 million.
items.canonical_answer: Spending exceeds receipts by N$12 million (1), so the government plans a budget deficit, not a measure of international trade (1).
marking_guidance: Context: budget; reasoning: difference 1; result: deficit/account distinction 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain why a balanced government budget does not prove goods exports equal goods imports.
items.canonical_answer: The budget compares government revenue and expenditure (1), while the trade balance compares international exports and imports, so the accounts differ (1).
marking_guidance: Confusion: public versus international accounts; boundary/test: transactions measured, 1 each.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Define an interest rate.
items.canonical_answer: The price of borrowing or reward for lending/saving relative to principal over a stated period.
marking_guidance: Meaning: financing price/reward 1; qualifier: relative principal and period 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain how a higher relevant borrowing rate can affect a firm’s planned credit-financed equipment purchase.
items.canonical_answer: Initial change: financing becomes more costly (1); the firm’s expected net return may fall, discouraging the purchase if other prospects are unchanged (1).
marking_guidance: Initial change 1; mechanism/effect for firm: dearer finance lowers attractiveness 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Explain why a policy-rate change need not immediately alter an existing fixed-rate loan payment.
items.canonical_answer: The existing contract may keep its rate unchanged for the stated term (1), so policy transmission to other borrowing conditions does not automatically rewrite that payment (1).
marking_guidance: Context: fixed-rate debt; reasoning: contract terms 1; result: no automatic payment change 1.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Define full employment.
items.canonical_answer: A policy objective of high use of available labour, with those willing and able to work able to find suitable employment without substantial involuntary joblessness.
marking_guidance: Meaning: A policy objective of high use of available labour, with those willing and able to work able to find suitable employment without substantial involuntary joblessness. Distinguishing feature: Full employment does not mean every person is employed or that short job-search transitions disappear. Award 1 for the core meaning and 1 for the precise qualifier.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Define price stability.
items.canonical_answer: A condition of a broadly stable general price level, commonly pursued through low and stable inflation.
marking_guidance: Meaning: A condition of a broadly stable general price level, commonly pursued through low and stable inflation. Distinguishing feature: Price stability concerns the general level and does not require each individual price to remain unchanged. Award 1 for the core meaning and 1 for the precise qualifier.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Define economic growth.
items.canonical_answer: An increase in a country’s real output (real GDP) over time.
marking_guidance: Meaning: increase in real output (real GDP) (1). Distinguishing feature: over time; growth per person also depends on population (1).
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Define redistribution of income.
items.canonical_answer: Changing the distribution of income between people or groups through measures such as taxes, transfers and services.
marking_guidance: Meaning: Changing the distribution of income between people or groups through measures such as taxes, transfers and services. Distinguishing feature: Redistribution can reduce hardship or inequality, while incentives, targeting and administrative resources affect its outcome. Award 1 for the core meaning and 1 for the precise qualifier.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Define balance of payments stability.
items.canonical_answer: A sustainable external-payments position without persistent financing pressures that disrupt economic activity.
marking_guidance: Meaning: A sustainable external-payments position without persistent financing pressures that disrupt economic activity. Distinguishing feature: External stability is not defined as equal merchandise exports and imports in each period or the absence of any individual account imbalance. Award 1 for the core meaning and 1 for the precise qualifier.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Define fiscal policy.
items.canonical_answer: Use of government spending and taxation to pursue economic objectives.
marking_guidance: Meaning: Use of government spending and taxation to pursue economic objectives. Distinguishing feature: Higher spending or lower taxes can support demand, but capacity, financing and implementation affect the result. Award 1 for the core meaning and 1 for the precise qualifier.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Define monetary policy.
items.canonical_answer: Use of monetary and credit conditions, including interest rates and money supply, to pursue economic objectives.
marking_guidance: Meaning: Use of monetary and credit conditions, including interest rates and money supply, to pursue economic objectives. Distinguishing feature: A policy-rate change may influence market rates and spending without ensuring every lender or borrower responds identically. Award 1 for the core meaning and 1 for the precise qualifier.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Define direct tax.
items.canonical_answer: A tax charged directly on income, profit or wealth of the liable person or organisation.
marking_guidance: Meaning: A tax charged directly on income, profit or wealth of the liable person or organisation. Distinguishing feature: The direct classification identifies the tax base and liability, not whether a tax is progressive or how its economic burden is ultimately shared. Award 1 for the core meaning and 1 for the precise qualifier.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Define indirect tax.
items.canonical_answer: A tax on spending or transactions in goods and services, commonly collected through suppliers.
marking_guidance: Meaning: A tax on spending or transactions in goods and services, commonly collected through suppliers. Distinguishing feature: An indirect tax can affect prices and producer receipts, with the actual burden depending on responses and market conditions. Award 1 for the core meaning and 1 for the precise qualifier.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Define progressive tax.
items.canonical_answer: A tax for which the proportion of income paid in tax rises as income rises.
marking_guidance: Meaning: A tax for which the proportion of income paid in tax rises as income rises. Distinguishing feature: Progressivity concerns the average income share paid, not merely a larger cash payment by a higher earner. Award 1 for the core meaning and 1 for the precise qualifier.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Define proportional tax.
items.canonical_answer: A tax whose rate remains a constant proportion of the relevant income or tax base.
marking_guidance: Meaning: A tax whose rate remains a constant proportion of the relevant income or tax base. Distinguishing feature: Equal tax rates generally produce larger cash payments on larger bases, so proportional does not mean equal tax amounts. Award 1 for the core meaning and 1 for the precise qualifier.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: Define regressive tax.
items.canonical_answer: A tax for which the proportion of income paid in tax falls as income rises.
marking_guidance: Meaning: A tax for which the proportion of income paid in tax falls as income rises. Distinguishing feature: A fixed cash payment can be regressive relative to income because it absorbs a larger share of a lower income. Award 1 for the core meaning and 1 for the precise qualifier.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: An economy has unused workers in some activities, but construction suppliers are already at capacity. A proposed budget increases maintenance spending and plans revenue N$120 million against spending N$132 million. Policymakers also want price stability and fairer access to services. (a) Describe three relevant policy features (6). (b) Examine possible effects and trade-offs (7). (c) Suggest a suitable implementation approach (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Spending is a fiscal instrument. The planned budget deficit is N$12 million. Employment, stable prices and access are objectives that can involve different constraints. (b) Implemented maintenance can support demand for suitable labour and materials. Capacity-constrained suppliers may raise prices or create delays, limiting real output response. Targeting services can improve access, but resources and financing have opportunity costs. The budget gap does not measure the trade balance. (c) Match work to available skills and materials, prioritise useful maintenance and monitor delivery and access. Stage activity where capacity would otherwise be overloaded. The judgement should support real useful output and distribution while limiting price pressure, rather than infer success from the spending amount alone.
marking_guidance: Context: proposed budget. Parts/allocation: (a) instrument, gap, objectives 2 each = 6. (b) demand mechanism 3, capacity price/delay 2, distribution/account limits 2 = 7. (c) resource targeting 3, staging/monitoring 2, conditional judgement 2 = 7.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum
items.repair_note: Step-6 Claude review: added standard examined content (named points, definitions, lists) missing from notes; corrected definition cards and template-garbled answers; removed author/tooling wording and invented/original labels.

items.prompt: (a) Define fiscal policy (2). (b) Define monetary policy (2). (c) Explain why an objective differs from an instrument (2). (d) Explain why a budget deficit differs from a goods-trade deficit (2). (e) Explain the distinction between proportional tax rate and equal cash tax (2). (f) Explain why real output matters to economic growth (2). (g) Explain why a borrowing-rate change may not change every existing payment (2). (h) Explain one limit on using spending to raise output (2).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Spending and taxation used for economic aims. (b) Monetary/credit conditions used for economic aims. (c) Outcome sought differs from means used. (d) Public revenue/spending differs from exports/imports. (e) Equal shares can produce different amounts when bases differ. (f) A money-value rise may reflect prices rather than more production. (g) Terms and fixed-rate arrangements can delay or prevent that payment change. (h) Capacity or implementation can constrain supply response.
marking_guidance: Parts/allocation and precision: eight 2-mark parts. (a/b) tool family + objective; (c) means/outcome; (d) accounts contrasted; (e) ratio/amount; (f) real/nominal distinction; (g) rate transmission/contract; (h) named condition + output consequence.
items.provenance: original Codex authoring from approved 6145 curriculum

items.prompt: The River Tools workshop plans a loan-financed expansion, but customer demand is uncertain. A higher relevant borrowing rate is announced. Separately, a public income-tax reduction is proposed to support household spending. Existing fixed-rate debt is unchanged under its terms. (a) Define an interest rate (2). (b) Explain the policy-family distinction between the two measures (4). (c) Explain how the measures could affect the workshop (7). (d) Discuss whether the tax proposal alone makes expansion advisable (7).
items.canonical_answer: (a) Borrowing price or saving/lending reward relative to principal and period. (b) The relevant-rate measure is monetary/credit; the tax change is fiscal. Both may affect spending but their instruments differ. (c) Higher new borrowing cost may reduce expected net returns. A tax reduction may leave customers more disposable income and support demand if they spend on the relevant output. Uncertain demand weakens the assumption of extra orders. Existing fixed-rate payments need not change. (d) Demand support is a potential benefit, but a proposal is not implementation and customers may save or buy elsewhere. New finance is dearer and orders remain uncertain. Expand only if realistic demand and complete repayment/cost evidence support it; the tax proposal alone is insufficient.
marking_guidance: Context: River Tools. Parts/allocation: (a) financing price/reward 1, principal/period 1. (b) monetary tool explanation 2, fiscal explanation 2 = 4. (c) borrowing mechanism 3, disposable-income route 2, expectations/contracts 2 = 7. (d) possible benefit 2, uncertainty/cost limits 2, conditional demand/finance judgement 3 = 7.

items.prompt: Evaluate whether a policymaker should judge a programme successful solely because total real output rises while population, income distribution and environmental costs are not reported (9).
items.canonical_answer: For: more real output can expand resources available for consumption, investment and services, supporting economic growth. Against: output per person depends on population, gains may be concentrated and external costs may offset benefits. Employment and price outcomes also need evidence. Judgement: recognise the output gain as one achievement but assess per-person resources, distribution and external costs before inferring broad improved living standards. The condition for that wider conclusion is evidence that gains are shared and relevant costs do not outweigh them. Total growth alone is insufficient.
marking_guidance: Argument for: real-resource mechanism, up to 4. Argument against: population/distribution/external limits, up to 4. Judgement: distinct shared-benefit and cost condition, 1. Total 9.
